The question of whether renewable energy sources can provide a stable power supply is contested across the retrieved evidence. Several sources emphasize the inherent instability of renewables: d1 notes that "sun, wind, tides and waves cannot be controlled to provide directly either continuous dispatchable power to meet base-load demand, or peak-load power when it is needed," and d7 states explicitly that "intermittent renewable energy sources cannot provide a stable power supply," increasing the need for energy reserves. [d6] similarly warns that "variations in electricity supply from renewable energy sources can result in occasions where there is either too little or too much electricity being produced," requiring costly standby conventional plants or large storage facilities. [d3] adds that "delivering a stable supply of electricity is getting more and more difficult, especially as households begin to contribute with electricity from solar panels and small wind turbines." On the other side, [d4] argues that Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) "can provide frequency regulation on a minute-by-minute basis to the grid, helping to keep a safe and stable power supply," and are becoming a viable solution for integrating variable renewables. [d2] further contends that distributed renewable energy systems backed by batteries "can provide fast backup power during calamities, making the energy system more resilient." In sum, while the evidence from [d1], [d3], [d6], and [d7] points to fundamental stability challenges with renewables, [d2] and [d4] suggest that emerging storage and grid technologies can enable renewables to contribute to a stable power supply, reflecting genuinely conflicting research outcomes and perspectives.
